title: Danish India
capsule: Danish India comprised a series of trading posts and colonial settlements established by the Danish East India Company from 1620, with Tharangambadi (Tranquebar) on the Coromandel Coast as the primary station, complemented by Serampore (Frederiksnagore) in Bengal and a claim to the Nicobar Islands. Denmark's colonial enterprise was chronically undercapitalized and operated in the margins of European trade, profiting chiefly as a neutral carrier during Anglo-Dutch wars rather than from monopoly control of commodities. Britain occupied Danish settlements twice during the Napoleonic Wars (1801–02 and 1808–15) when Denmark sided with France; Serampore was sold to Britain in 1839, and Tranquebar together with most remaining stations in 1845. The Nicobar Islands were formally ceded in October 1868 and annexed by Britain in 1869, ending two and a half centuries of Danish presence in the subcontinent.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The locations of Danish factories and the dates of acquisition and sale are documented in company and colonial records; territorial extent was never defined by inland boundaries and was limited to coastal enclaves, making precise mapping straightforward for the settlements but inapplicable to hinterland claims.
